title: Lesson 12: Squaring
subtopics: Digit sums of squares and square roots of perfect squares
Three and four-figure numbers by longer duplexes
learningGoals: Square numbers quickly by choosing the right pattern instead of defaulting to long multiplication.
Use duplexes and splitting to extend squaring methods from two digits to much larger numbers.
Check or recover square information through digit clues and square-root reasoning.
coreIdeas: Several special squaring cases are short front-and-back patterns, but they all connect to the same deeper duplex structure.
When a number sits near a friendly anchor like 50, the anchor and the distance from it do most of the work.
Even larger squares and algebraic squares follow the same left-middle-right logic, which keeps the lesson unified.

workedExamples.method: Use 7 x 8 for the left block and append 25 to get 5625.
Use the deficiency 3 from 50: left part 25 - 3 = 22 and right part 3^2 = 09.
Use duplexes 16, 24, and 9 and merge them to 1849.
This confirms the correct square-root candidate for 6889 by direct squaring.

starterPractice: Warm-up: square 55 by saying the changing left block and fixed right block.
Guided: square 47 using the deficiency from 50.

onboarding.coachIntro: Raj checks language comfort, current confidence, and session goal before starting Squaring.
onboarding.placementRule: Recommended start level for Lesson 12: confident. If the learner struggles twice in one step, keep the pace slow and repeat the pattern with a smaller number.

mission.missionPromise: Square numbers quickly by choosing the right pattern instead of defaulting to long multiplication.
mission.successCelebration: Celebrate each correct step in Squaring with points, a badge pulse, and a quick coach line before moving on.

microLessonPattern: Coach opens with one short hook and names the pattern.
Coach models one worked move on the board.
Coach reads the exercise question aloud.
Niagh tries before the full answer is shown.
Instant feedback either celebrates or repairs the first mistake.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise A: Squaring numbers ending in 5
sessionFlow.coachHook: For a number ending in 5, multiply the part before the 5 by one more than itself, and place 25 on the right.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Write 75 squared as 7 and 5, then compute 7 x 8 for the left block and append 25.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why does seventy-five squared become fifty-six twenty-five?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why does seventy-five squared become fifty-six twenty-five?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Squaring numbers ending in 5 is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The last two digits will always be 25.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Square 55, 15, and 95 by saying the left block before the full answer.

sessionFlow.coachHook: For numbers near 50, adjust 25 by the amount above or below 50 for the left part, and square that small amount for the right part.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Show 53 squared and 47 squared side by side, with one board half for above 50 and one for below 50.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: How do the same near-50 ideas work for both fifty-three squared and forty-seven squared?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: How do the same near-50 ideas work for both fifty-three squared and forty-seven squared?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Squaring numbers near 50 is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The distance from fifty is the key number.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Square 56, 44, and 42 by saying the adjustment from 50 first.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise C: General squaring with duplexes
sessionFlow.coachHook: General squaring uses duplexes: outer squares on the ends and doubled products in the middle, merged from left to right.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Write 43 squared, compute D(4), D(43), and D(3), then merge 16, 24, and 9.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: How do the duplexes of a two-digit number produce the full square?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: How do the duplexes of a two-digit number produce the full square?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. General squaring with duplexes is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: There will be three duplexes for a two-digit number.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Square 64, 31, and 23 by naming the three duplexes before the answer.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise D: Number splitting and algebraic squaring
sessionFlow.coachHook: Number splitting lets a long square behave like a smaller one, and the same duplex structure carries directly into algebraic squaring.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Show 123 squared as 12 slash 3, then place x plus 5 over itself to show the matching algebraic pattern.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why do number splitting and algebraic squaring both still follow the same duplex pattern?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why do number splitting and algebraic squaring both still follow the same duplex pattern?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Number splitting and algebraic squaring is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Grouping changes the bookkeeping, not the pattern.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Square 123 and 312 by splitting, then explain x plus 5 squared in the same left-middle-right way.

sessionFlow.subtopic: Digit sums of squares and square roots of perfect squares
sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise E: Digit sums of squares and square roots of perfect squares
sessionFlow.coachHook: Digit sums help check squares, and square roots of four-digit perfect squares are found by combining a front-digit estimate with a last-digit test.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Show 6889 and 5776, mark the first two digits to estimate the tens place, then test the last digit and choose between the two candidates.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: How do the first digits, last digit, and digit-sum check work together when finding a square root?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: How do the first digits, last digit, and digit-sum check work together when finding a square root?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Digit sums of squares and square roots of perfect squares is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: A four-digit square has a two-digit root.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Choose between 83 and 87 for the root of 6889, then choose between 74 and 76 for 5776.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise F: Three and four-figure numbers by longer duplexes
sessionFlow.coachHook: Larger squares use longer duplex chains, but the symmetry is unchanged: the square is the total of its duplexes merged in order.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Work 341 squared and 4332 squared by listing all duplexes from the outside inward and then merging them one by one.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why does a larger square still reduce to a chain of duplexes rather than a completely new method?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, try this one. Say your first step, then your answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why does a larger square still reduce to a chain of duplexes rather than a completely new method?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. Three and four-figure numbers by longer duplexes is now stronger and ready for the next step.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Square 212 and 131 by listing the duplex chain first, then merge to the full answer.

screenplay.teacherLine: Numbers ending in five have a very short squaring route.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 75^2 with the 7 and 5 separated visually.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does seventy-five squared become fifty-six twenty-five?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The last two digits will always be 25.

screenplay.teacherLine: Take the number before the five, here seven, and multiply it by the next number, eight.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 7 x 8 = 56 as the left block.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does seventy-five squared become fifty-six twenty-five?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The right block is fixed at 25.

screenplay.teacherLine: So seventy-five squared is fifty-six twenty-five, or 5625.
screenplay.boardAction: Join 56 and 25 into 5625 and box it.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does seventy-five squared become fifty-six twenty-five?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The method is left block plus 25.

screenplay.teacherLine: Now square ninety-five using the same two-step routine.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 9 x 10 = __ and keep 25 ready on the right.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does seventy-five squared become fifty-six twenty-five?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Nine times ten gives the left block 90.

screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what part changes and what part never changes when a number ends in five?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave changing left block and fixed 25 on the board.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does seventy-five squared become fifty-six twenty-five?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: The left block changes, and the right block is always 25.
screenplay.fallbackHint: That single sentence captures the method.

screenplay.teacherLine: A number close to fifty can be squared by using its small distance from fifty.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 53^2 and mark +3 from 50.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the same near-50 ideas work for both fifty-three squared and forty-seven squared?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The distance from fifty is the key number.

screenplay.teacherLine: For fifty-three squared, increase twenty-five by three to get twenty-eight, and square three to get zero-nine.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the same near-50 ideas work for both fifty-three squared and forty-seven squared?
screenplay.fallbackHint: This gives 2809.

screenplay.teacherLine: For forty-seven squared, the deficiency is three, so reduce the left part to twenty-two and keep zero-nine on the right.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the same near-50 ideas work for both fifty-three squared and forty-seven squared?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Below fifty means subtract the deficiency from 25.

screenplay.teacherLine: Now square forty-four by this method.
screenplay.boardAction: Show deficiency 6 from 50 and leave 25 - 6 and 6^2 blank.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the same near-50 ideas work for both fifty-three squared and forty-seven squared?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Left part 19, right part 36.

screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: when do you add to 25 and when do you subtract from 25?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave above 50 and below 50 as two labeled arrows.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the same near-50 ideas work for both fifty-three squared and forty-seven squared?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: Add when the number is above 50 and subtract when it is below 50.
screenplay.fallbackHint: The right part is always the square of the distance.

screenplay.teacherLine: The general squaring method is the square-version of vertical and crosswise multiplication.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 43^2 and label three duplex positions.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the duplexes of a two-digit number produce the full square?
screenplay.fallbackHint: There will be three duplexes for a two-digit number.

screenplay.teacherLine: For forty-three, D of four is sixteen, D of forty-three is twenty-four, and D of three is nine.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 16, 24, and 9 under the number.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the duplexes of a two-digit number produce the full square?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The middle duplex is twice the product of the two digits.

screenplay.teacherLine: Merge sixteen, twenty-four, and nine to get eighteen forty-nine.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 16,24 becoming 184 and then 184,9 becoming 1849.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the duplexes of a two-digit number produce the full square?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The merging is the same carry process used earlier.

screenplay.teacherLine: Now square sixty-four using duplexes.
screenplay.boardAction: Show D(6), D(64), and D(4) with blanks.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the duplexes of a two-digit number produce the full square?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The duplexes are 36, 48, and 16.

screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what is a duplex of two digits in one sentence?
screenplay.boardAction: Box the phrase twice the product.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the duplexes of a two-digit number produce the full square?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: It is twice the product of the two digits.
screenplay.fallbackHint: That definition powers the middle step.

screenplay.teacherLine: Sometimes a large number becomes friendlier if we group digits before squaring.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 123 as 12 / 3.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do number splitting and algebraic squaring both still follow the same duplex pattern?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Grouping changes the bookkeeping, not the pattern.

screenplay.teacherLine: For one hundred twenty-three squared, the grouped duplexes are 144, 72, and 9, which merge to 15129.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do number splitting and algebraic squaring both still follow the same duplex pattern?
screenplay.fallbackHint: This is the same left-middle-right structure.

screenplay.teacherLine: The same structure appears in algebra: x plus 5 squared becomes x squared, ten x, and twenty-five.
screenplay.boardAction: Write x^2, 10x, and 25 in three answer slots.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do number splitting and algebraic squaring both still follow the same duplex pattern?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Only the symbols changed; the structure did not.

screenplay.teacherLine: Now square three hundred twelve by grouping it as three slash twelve.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 3^2, 2 x 3 x 12, and 12^2 with blanks.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do number splitting and algebraic squaring both still follow the same duplex pattern?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The grouped blocks are 9, 72, and 144.

screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what three positions always appear in these split or algebraic squares?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave left, middle, right labeled on the board.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why do number splitting and algebraic squaring both still follow the same duplex pattern?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: A left square, a doubled middle product, and a right square.
screenplay.fallbackHint: That is the whole pattern.

screenplay.subtopic: Digit sums of squares and square roots of perfect squares
screenplay.teacherLine: A perfect square leaves clues in both its front digits and its last digit.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 6889 and split it as 68 | 89.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the first digits, last digit, and digit-sum check work together when finding a square root?
screenplay.fallbackHint: A four-digit square has a two-digit root.

screenplay.subtopic: Digit sums of squares and square roots of perfect squares
screenplay.teacherLine: Because sixty-eight sits between sixty-four and eighty-one, the first digit of the root must be eight.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 8^2 = 64 and 9^2 = 81 beside 68.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the first digits, last digit, and digit-sum check work together when finding a square root?
screenplay.fallbackHint: So the root is eighty-something.

screenplay.subtopic: Digit sums of squares and square roots of perfect squares
screenplay.teacherLine: The last digit nine means the root ends in three or seven, so test eighty-three and eighty-seven; eighty-three squared is 6889, so the root is eighty-three.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 83 and 87 as the two candidates, then confirm 83 x 83 = 6889.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the first digits, last digit, and digit-sum check work together when finding a square root?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Digit sums or the midpoint square can eliminate the wrong candidate.

screenplay.subtopic: Digit sums of squares and square roots of perfect squares
screenplay.teacherLine: Now decide whether the square root of 5776 is seventy-four or seventy-six.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 7^2 = 49 and 8^2 = 64 beside 57, then mark last-digit options 4 or 6.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the first digits, last digit, and digit-sum check work together when finding a square root?
screenplay.fallbackHint: 76^2 is 5776, and it is above 75.

screenplay.subtopic: Digit sums of squares and square roots of perfect squares
screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what three clues do you read before naming a two-digit square root?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave front digits, last digit, check as three boxes.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the first digits, last digit, and digit-sum check work together when finding a square root?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: Use the front digits for the first figure, the last digit for two choices, then test which one fits.
screenplay.fallbackHint: That three-clue method keeps the root mental.

screenplay.subtopic: Three and four-figure numbers by longer duplexes
screenplay.teacherLine: A longer number simply has more duplexes, not a different squaring rule.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 341^2 with duplex slots D(3), D(34), D(341), D(41), D(1).
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does a larger square still reduce to a chain of duplexes rather than a completely new method?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The chain grows symmetrically.

screenplay.subtopic: Three and four-figure numbers by longer duplexes
screenplay.teacherLine: For three hundred forty-one the duplexes are 9, 24, 22, 8, and 1, which merge to 116281.
screenplay.boardAction: Write the duplex values under each slot and merge them step by step.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does a larger square still reduce to a chain of duplexes rather than a completely new method?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Each new duplex is attached with the same carry logic.

screenplay.subtopic: Three and four-figure numbers by longer duplexes
screenplay.teacherLine: For four thousand three hundred thirty-two squared the duplex chain is longer, but it still merges in the same left-to-right way.
screenplay.boardAction: List the seven duplex totals for 4332^2 and then build 18766224.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does a larger square still reduce to a chain of duplexes rather than a completely new method?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Longer does not mean different.

screenplay.subtopic: Three and four-figure numbers by longer duplexes
screenplay.teacherLine: Now square two hundred twelve using the larger-number duplex pattern.
screenplay.boardAction: Show the duplex slots with blanks for 212.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does a larger square still reduce to a chain of duplexes rather than a completely new method?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The duplex chain is 4, 4, 9, 4, 4.

screenplay.subtopic: Three and four-figure numbers by longer duplexes
screenplay.teacherLine: Final checkpoint: what stays unchanged from 43 squared all the way up to 4332 squared?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave duplex chain plus merge written under both examples.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does a larger square still reduce to a chain of duplexes rather than a completely new method?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: We still find duplexes and merge them in order.
screenplay.fallbackHint: That is the unified squaring method.

teachingFlowStages.intent: Show that squaring has several fast board patterns before the general method appears.
Explain end-in-5, near-50, duplex, splitting, and square-root clue methods with visible board structure.
Demonstrate both short special cases and longer duplex chains so the lesson scales naturally.
Have the learner state the pattern first, then compute the square.
Mix direct squares, larger squares, and reverse square-root checks.
Use digit clues, candidate testing, and careful block merging to avoid square errors.
Require the learner to explain why several different-looking square methods are still connected.
